title: How to Survive a Stock Collapse: What Founders Get Wrong About Going Public | Dave CEO Jason Wilk
guest: Jason Wilk, founder and CEO of Dave (fintech/neobank)
summary: Jason Wilk, serial entrepreneur and CEO of Dave, explains how a personal pain point with overdraft fees led him to build a neobank with no banking experience, and how the company survived a 98% stock collapse after its SPAC by leaning on a clear mission, zero employee churn and a single profitability metric (2.1 million paying members) that drove a 900% rebound. He also covers Dave's cash-flow and AI underwriting (loss rates from 10-20% down to about 1%), the tipping model, the fintech winter as a moat, his Mark Cuban origin story, and advice that cutting expenses is the best ROI for people living paycheck to paycheck.

ideas.idea: The best companies start when the founder is solving a real personal pain point.
ideas.detail: Wilk was constantly overdrafting his checking account while starting his first business, paying $34 and up to $100 a day in fees; after selling that company he used his cushion to attack the problem.

ideas.idea: Banks charge high overdraft and monthly fees because a basic checking account costs them about $300 a year to maintain, so a digital-first neobank with its own tech stack and no branches can save customers millions in fees.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Younger, thin-file customers who cannot get a JPMorgan credit card are only profitable to legacy banks through fees; Dave's customers on average pay $400 a year in bank fees.

ideas.idea: You do not need domain experience to disrupt an industry; a dedicated entrepreneur working seven days a week learns faster than an MBA's couple of hours of class a day.
ideas.detail: Wilk had no banking or fintech background and had to convince banks and processors to work with Dave when bank partnerships, debit processing and ACH for small-dollar lending barely existed; 'anyone can do it.'

ideas.idea: Second-time founders are much more successful because hiring, firing, fundraising and growth planning become muscle memory.
ideas.detail: His Y Combinator company taught him to raise capital and meet investors like Mark Cuban, so Dave got 'off to the races' much faster; the hosts call this chutzpah built from prior exits.

ideas.idea: Twenty years of competitive golf, a self-sufficient individual sport, built the thick skin, self-belief and grit that transfer directly to entrepreneurship.
ideas.detail: His original goal was to go pro; when he was not good enough, redirecting the same determination into business was an easy transition and he says he has never questioned his self-belief. He also grew up middle class with no backstop, always needing a job after school and never living beyond his means.

ideas.idea: A published mission, vision, strategy and defined audience is what holds a company together when the stock collapses; a high stock price is a byproduct, not the goal.
ideas.detail: Dave's seed deck was about disrupting overdraft fees with no IPO timeline; when the stock fell 98% there was essentially no employee churn because the team was mission-aligned rather than purely equity-motivated, and they were still helping millions buy gas and groceries.

ideas.idea: Public-market investors are completely different from VCs: most VCs are looking for the exit door, so going public before building a solid public shareholder base leaves you exposed.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Wilk does not regret the SPAC route but says the market fell out from under Dave as rates rose and growth stocks sold off before it had a foundation of public investors; the only frustration was timing.

ideas.idea: Being even-keeled, never too high on good news or too low on bad, is what gets a leader through a crisis.
ideas.detail: There was no 'I'll show you' mentality and no one to point fingers at in a macro-driven event with tens of thousands of investors; he just kept the focus on delivering the growth plan.

ideas.idea: Simplify the profitability story to one clear metric, report progress against it every quarter, and the market will eventually reward you.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: With investor Imran's help, Dave told the Street it would be profitable at 2.1 million monthly paying members; when it hit that number the stock rose about 900% in a year.

ideas.idea: When interest rates rise, investors write money-losing companies down to zero on fear of dilutive capital raises, so profitability becomes the only thing that matters.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Growth at all costs was rewarded in 2021-2022; Dave pivoted to gross-margin improvement and contract renegotiation on an expedited basis without any layoffs.

ideas.idea: In a crisis, communicate from the fundamentals: customers only care that the lights stay on, and the board and team get a calm, collective unpacking of what is actually happening.
ideas.detail: No customer ever wrote in asking about the stock; the business was better six months after going public than before, so there was nothing to blame internally beyond margins.

ideas.idea: A downturn can build a moat: when VC funding dries up, smaller competitors die and the leaders take share, and high rates push credit-denied customers to alternative products.
ideas.detail: Seeing a fintech with 12 million consumers trade at a $50 million market cap shut off venture markets for Dave's competitors; big banks cutting credit cards and personal loans sent new customers to Dave. Patience was well worth it.

ideas.idea: Underwriting on cash-flow data instead of FICO scores lets thin-file customers get credit based on their paycheck and solvency between paychecks.
ideas.detail: Dave pioneered this in 2017 as an alternative to the 'unintelligent' flat $34 overdraft fee charged regardless of overdraft size.

ideas.idea: AI models trained on billions of transaction data points (Dave's 'Cash AI') cut loss rates from 10-20% to about 1% while quadrupling average loan size from $50 to over $200.
ideas.detail: Hundreds of features such as where you bank, merchant types and even the time you buy food feed the model; loss rates have improved eight quarters in a row, and at nearly $2 billion originated per quarter every 10 basis points matters for profitability.

ideas.idea: A direct-to-consumer public company should resist becoming B2B while in recovery mode because investor clarity about who you serve drives valuation.
ideas.detail: Wilk is asked constantly about licensing the underwriting model but says mixing D2C and B2B muddies the story; instead Dave plans longer-duration loans for things like plane tickets and school books.

ideas.idea: In a regulated industry you must genuinely believe in the products you ship, and expect to have to educate regulators used to legacy models.
ideas.detail: Dave's original free-to-borrow, optional-tip model drew regulatory scrutiny ('who would tip a financial institution?'), but it makes sense for customers paying $400 a year in overdraft fees; tips averaged a few dollars and Dave has donated over $20 million to Feeding America.

ideas.idea: For anyone living paycheck to paycheck, the best return on investment is cutting expenses by 10-20%, not a magic investment or crypto token.
ideas.detail: Quoting Mark Cuban; Dave's data shows customers spend about $400 a year on bank fees, which is a good place to start. The hosts note most advice jumps to investing when expense management comes first.

ideas.idea: Writing publicly about people you admire and then emailing them can start a mentor relationship that leads to your first check.
ideas.detail: In 2008 Wilk blogged about Mark Cuban's TechCrunch 40 keynote on ten ways to get him to invest, emailed the post to the address Cuban gave the crowd, kept pitching ideas, and Cuban became Dave's first check; Cuban later called him a great investment on stage in front of 150 people.
